audience.summary: For students who know basic Python and want to build a real database application: a Flask web app on top of a SQLite database, with the SQL written by hand so every query can be read and explained.
knowledge: Basic HTML: forms, links and tables.
What a table, a row and a column are in a database; SQL is explained as you go.
Using a terminal to run commands.

architecture.summary: A server-rendered Flask app. Each request is matched to a view function, which validates the input, reads or writes the SQLite database through one data-access module, and renders an HTML template. Settings come from app_config.json and environment variables. Every form carries a CSRF token, and every query passes values as parameters.

layers.label: Start-up
layers.description: run.py and create_app() build the app: settings, database, security checks, pages and error pages.

layers.label: Pages
layers.description: Flask blueprints with one view function per page, and the Jinja templates and CSS they render.

layers.label: Rules
layers.description: Validation of form input and the CSRF and security-header checks that run on every request.

layers.label: Data
layers.description: The data-access module with every SQL query, the connection and commands, and the schema.

components.name: Application factory
components.responsibility: run.py calls create_app(), which loads .env and app_config.json, chooses the database path and secret key, registers the database commands, security checks, blueprints and error pages, and prepares the database.

components.name: Settings
components.responsibility: Reads and checks app_config.json (name, institution, page size, sample data), loads KEY=VALUE lines from .env without replacing variables that are already set, and creates the secret key once in instance/secret_key.

components.name: Routes (view functions)
components.responsibility: One blueprint per area. Each function reads the request, calls validation and the repository, then renders a template or redirects with a flash message (Post/Redirect/Get). Deleting is a GET confirmation page plus a POST.

components.name: Templates and styles
components.responsibility: Jinja templates extend base.html, which has the navigation, flash messages and skip link. _macros.html builds labelled form fields with errors linked by aria-describedby. Jinja escapes everything it inserts. style.css holds the accent colour.

components.name: Validation
components.responsibility: Pure functions that clean form input (trimming, upper-casing roll numbers) and return the values and a dictionary of errors by field. No Flask and no database, so they are easy to test.

components.name: CSRF and security headers
components.responsibility: Gives each session a random token that every form must send back; a POST without it is refused with 400. Adds a Content-Security-Policy that allows no scripts, and other security headers, to every response.

components.name: Data access
components.responsibility: Every SQL query: searching, filtering, sorting and paging students, creating, updating and deleting rows, enrollments, the attendance upsert and statistics. Values always go in as parameters; ORDER BY columns come from a fixed dictionary.

components.name: Connection and commands
components.responsibility: Opens connections with foreign keys on and rows by column name, creates the tables, adds the fictional sample data to a new database file, and provides the init-db, seed-db, reset-db and backup-db commands.

components.name: Database schema
components.responsibility: Four tables: students and courses, enrollments joining them (many-to-many, primary key on both ids) and attendance, which refers to an enrollment. Foreign keys cascade deletes; UNIQUE and CHECK constraints back up the validation.

components.name: Tests
components.responsibility: pytest tests on a temporary database with a fixed date: validation, configuration, queries and constraints, every page through Flask's test client with real CSRF tokens, the database commands and the security behaviour.

connections.label: Loads the settings and secret key
Registers the checks for every request
Refuses a POST without the CSRF token before the view runs
Builds a fresh app per test

steps.text: students/form.html renders the form with a hidden csrf_token field and a labelled input for each field.
When the form is posted, check_csrf() compares the token with the one in the session and refuses the request if they differ.
new_student() passes the form to validate_student().
validate_student() cleans the values and returns errors by field, for example a future admission date.
With no errors, create_student() runs an INSERT with named parameters. A UNIQUE failure on the roll number becomes a form error.
The view flashes “Added …” and redirects to the student's page, so reloading doesn't submit the form again.
mark() validates the date: not in the future, written as YYYY-MM-DD.
attendance_sheet() joins enrollments, students and that day's marks, with a LEFT JOIN so unmarked students appear too.
attendance/mark.html shows present, late and absent radio buttons for each student.
On POST, mark() keeps only fields named status-<id> with a known status.
save_attendance() skips students who don't take the course and upserts each mark with INSERT … ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE.
The Delete link opens a confirmation page (GET) that counts the enrollments and attendance marks that will go too.
The confirmation form posts the CSRF token; only that POST deletes.
delete_student() runs one DELETE on students.
ON DELETE CASCADE removes the student's enrollments, and through them their attendance, because connect() turned foreign keys on.

walkthrough.title: Starting the app
walkthrough.role: The file you run: builds the app and starts Flask's development server.
walkthrough.explanation: run.py imports create_app() and builds the app at import time, so `flask --app studentms` commands and run.py use the same set-up. When run directly, it reads HOST (default 127.0.0.1, so only this computer can connect) and PORT (default 5000) and calls app.run(). Debug mode is off unless FLASK_DEBUG=1, because the debugger would let anyone who can reach the app run code.

symbols.name: app
symbols.explanation: The Flask application object, created by create_app().

walkthrough.title: The application factory
walkthrough.role: create_app() builds and configures the Flask app.
walkthrough.explanation: create_app() loads .env, creates the Flask object with instance/ as its instance folder and sets the configuration: the parsed app_config.json (APP), the database path, debug mode, cookie settings (HttpOnly, SameSite=Lax) and a 1 MB limit on request bodies. Tests pass overrides such as a temporary DATABASE and a fixed TODAY. It then registers the teardown that closes connections, the database commands, the security checks, prepares the database, registers the four blueprints, makes the settings available to every template and sets one error page for 400, 404, 405, 413 and 500.

symbols.name: create_app
symbols.explanation: Builds the app; called by run.py, the flask command and every test.

symbols.name: _error_page
symbols.explanation: Renders errors/error.html with the status code; for 500 it logs the exception first.

walkthrough.title: Settings and the secret key
walkthrough.role: Reads app_config.json and .env, and provides the secret key.
walkthrough.explanation: parse_config() turns the JSON into a frozen AppConfig dataclass and raises ConfigError with a clear message for each wrong value; True is rejected as a page size because bool is a subclass of int in Python. load_env_file() is a small .env reader: it skips comments and blank lines and uses os.environ.setdefault, so real environment variables win. secret_key() returns SECRET_KEY if set, otherwise reads or creates a random 64-character key in instance/secret_key with owner-only permissions.

symbols.name: AppConfig
symbols.explanation: The checked settings: app_name, institution_name, author_name, students_per_page, seed_demo_data.

symbols.name: parse_config
symbols.explanation: Validates a dict from the JSON file.

symbols.name: load_env_file
symbols.explanation: Reads .env without overwriting variables that are already set.

symbols.name: secret_key
symbols.explanation: SECRET_KEY, or a random key created once in instance/secret_key.

walkthrough.title: The database schema
walkthrough.explanation: Every statement uses IF NOT EXISTS, so the file can run on every start without losing data. students and courses have INTEGER PRIMARY KEY AUTOINCREMENT ids; roll_number, email and code are UNIQUE COLLATE NOCASE. enrollments has a composite primary key (student_id, course_id) and foreign keys with ON DELETE CASCADE. attendance has the key (student_id, course_id, date) and a composite foreign key to enrollments, so a mark can't exist for a student who doesn't take the course. CHECK constraints limit status values and credits. Indexes speed up filtering by class, sorting by name and looking up a course's marks by date.

walkthrough.title: Connections, sample data and commands
walkthrough.role: Opens connections, creates the tables, seeds sample data and defines the database commands.
walkthrough.explanation: connect() sets row_factory = sqlite3.Row (so code can write row["first_name"]) and runs PRAGMA foreign_keys = ON, which SQLite needs on every connection for cascades to work. get_db() keeps one connection per request in Flask's g object; close_db() closes it after the request. prepare_database() runs at start-up: it creates missing tables and seeds only a database file that didn't exist before, so a database emptied on purpose stays empty. seed_db() builds deterministic sample attendance from a formula. backup_db() uses SQLite's backup API, which is safe while the app runs; reset-db always backs up first and asks for --yes.

symbols.name: connect
symbols.explanation: Opens a connection with rows by column name and foreign keys on.

symbols.name: get_db
symbols.explanation: The current request's connection, opened on first use.

symbols.name: prepare_database
symbols.explanation: Creates tables, and seeds a new database file when seed_demo_data is true.

symbols.name: seed_db
symbols.explanation: Adds the fictional courses, students, enrollments and ten school days of marks.

symbols.name: backup_db
symbols.explanation: Copies the database into a timestamped file in instance/backups.

symbols.name: register_commands
symbols.explanation: Defines the init-db, seed-db, reset-db and backup-db commands for flask --app studentms.

walkthrough.title: Every SQL query
walkthrough.role: All reading and writing of data, always with parameters.
walkthrough.explanation: list_students() builds a WHERE clause from the search and filters, counts the matches, then fetches one page with LIMIT ? OFFSET ?. The search matches the full name with first_name || ' ' || last_name, and like_pattern() escapes % and _ with ESCAPE '\'. Sorting picks SQL from SORT_COLUMNS because ORDER BY can't take a parameter. create_student() and update_student() catch sqlite3.IntegrityError and turn a UNIQUE failure into a DuplicateError for the form. save_attendance() upserts marks. statistics() computes every dashboard figure with COUNT, SUM and GROUP BY; ATTENDED counts present and late.

symbols.name: list_students
symbols.explanation: One page of matching students and the total count.

symbols.name: like_pattern
symbols.explanation: A LIKE pattern that matches the text anywhere, with % and _ matched literally.

symbols.name: SORT_COLUMNS
symbols.explanation: The only ORDER BY clauses allowed.

symbols.name: DuplicateError
symbols.explanation: A unique value is already used; carries the field name for the form.

symbols.name: save_attendance
symbols.explanation: Upserts one mark per enrolled student for the day.

symbols.name: statistics
symbols.explanation: Counts and attendance rates for the dashboard and statistics page.

walkthrough.title: Validating forms
walkthrough.role: Checks and cleans what people type.
walkthrough.explanation: Each validator takes the submitted form (any mapping, so tests can pass a plain dict) and returns a Result with cleaned values and errors by field name. _clean() trims text and collapses inner spaces. Roll numbers are upper-cased and must match ROLL_PATTERN; an empty email becomes None so the UNIQUE constraint ignores it; admission dates must be real calendar dates (parse_date rejects 2023-02-29) and not in the future. validate_course() checks the code pattern and that credits are a whole number from 1 to 10.

symbols.name: Result
symbols.explanation: values and errors, with ok when there are no errors.

symbols.name: validate_student
symbols.explanation: Checks every student field and cleans the values.

symbols.name: validate_course
symbols.explanation: Checks the course code, title, credits and description.

symbols.name: parse_date
symbols.explanation: A real date written as YYYY-MM-DD, or None.

walkthrough.title: CSRF protection and headers
walkthrough.role: Stops forged form submissions and adds security headers.
walkthrough.explanation: csrf_token() stores a random token in the signed session the first time a page needs it; templates put it in a hidden field. check_csrf() runs before every request and aborts a POST with 400 unless the form's token matches the session's, compared with hmac.compare_digest so the time taken reveals nothing. add_security_headers() sets a Content-Security-Policy that allows only this app's own styles and no scripts at all, plus nosniff and a same-origin referrer policy.

symbols.name: csrf_token
symbols.explanation: The session's token, created on first use; available in templates.

symbols.name: check_csrf
symbols.explanation: Refuses a POST without the right token.

symbols.name: CONTENT_SECURITY_POLICY
symbols.explanation: What the browser may load: this app's files only, and no scripts.

walkthrough.title: The student pages
walkthrough.role: List, add, view, edit and delete students, and manage their enrollments.
walkthrough.explanation: list_students() turns query-string values into a StudentQuery, accepting only known statuses and sort keys, and redirects past the last page to the last one. new_student() and edit_student() share the form template: on POST they validate, save and redirect, or render the form again with status 400 and the errors. delete_student() shows a confirmation page on GET and deletes only on POST. enroll() and unenroll() are POST-only and flash what happened.

symbols.name: list_students
symbols.explanation: Search, filters, sorting and pages for the student list.

symbols.name: new_student
symbols.explanation: Shows and handles the add-student form.

symbols.name: delete_student
symbols.explanation: Confirmation on GET; the delete on POST.

symbols.name: enroll
symbols.explanation: Adds the student to the chosen course.

walkthrough.title: Marking attendance
walkthrough.role: The attendance sheet for a course and day.
walkthrough.explanation: mark() reads the date from the query string or the form and refuses future dates with a flash message. On GET it renders the sheet: every active student taking the course, with today's mark or Present by default. On POST it collects fields named status-<student id>, ignoring anything else and unknown statuses, saves them and redirects back to the same day.

symbols.name: choose
symbols.explanation: Lists the courses to mark.

symbols.name: mark
symbols.explanation: Shows and saves the sheet for one course and day.

walkthrough.title: Dashboard, statistics and health
walkthrough.role: The home page, the statistics page and the health check.
walkthrough.explanation: index() and statistics() render figures from repository.statistics(), calculated from the data on every request. health() answers {"status": "ok"} only after reading the students table, so it proves the database works; scripts and CampusKit's verification use it to know the app has started.

symbols.name: index
symbols.explanation: The dashboard.

symbols.name: health
symbols.explanation: Answers 200 with JSON when the database can be read.

walkthrough.title: Accessible form fields
walkthrough.role: Jinja macros for labelled fields, the error summary and percentages.
walkthrough.explanation: field() renders a label, an optional hint and the input; when there is an error it adds aria-invalid="true" and links the hint and error with aria-describedby, so screen readers read them with the field. error_summary() lists every problem at the top of the form with links to the fields. percent() shows “No marks yet” instead of dividing by zero.

walkthrough.title: Test set-up
walkthrough.role: Builds a fresh app with a temporary database for each test.
walkthrough.explanation: make_app() calls create_app() with overrides: a test secret key, a database file in pytest's tmp_path, five students per page and a fixed date (21 October 2026), so tests never touch your real data and give the same result every day. csrf_from() opens a page and reads the token from its form with a regular expression, as a browser would, and post_form() submits a form with it.

symbols.name: make_app
symbols.explanation: An app with its own temporary database and a fixed date.

symbols.name: csrf_from
symbols.explanation: Reads the CSRF token from a page's form.

symbols.name: post_form
symbols.explanation: Submits a form with a valid token.

viva.question: What does your project do?
viva.answer: It keeps student records in a SQLite database: students, courses, enrollments and daily attendance. You can add, edit and delete students and courses, search and filter the student list, mark attendance and see statistics, through a Flask web app that runs on your own computer.

viva.question: Why did you choose Flask and SQLite?
viva.answer: Flask is a small Python web framework where each URL maps to a Python function, which keeps the code easy to follow. SQLite is a full SQL database in one file and is built into Python, so there's no database server to install. Both suit one user on one computer.

viva.question: Explain the database design.
viva.answer: There are four tables. students and courses each have an integer id. enrollments links them, because a student takes many courses and a course has many students: a many-to-many relationship with the primary key (student_id, course_id). attendance has one row per student, course and day and refers to an enrollment, so a mark can only exist for an enrolled student.

viva.question: What is the difference between a primary key and a foreign key?
viva.answer: A primary key uniquely identifies each row of its own table, like students.id. A foreign key is a column that refers to the primary key of another table, like enrollments.student_id referring to students.id. The database refuses a foreign key value that doesn't exist in the other table.

keyConcepts.label: Foreign key refers to another table

viva.question: What happens to a student's attendance when you delete the student?
viva.answer: It's deleted automatically. enrollments.student_id has ON DELETE CASCADE, so deleting the student deletes their enrollments, and attendance refers to enrollments with ON DELETE CASCADE too. SQLite only enforces this because connect() runs PRAGMA foreign_keys = ON on every connection. The confirmation page shows how many marks will go.

keyConcepts.label: Foreign keys must be switched on

viva.question: How do you protect against SQL injection?
viva.answer: Every query passes values as parameters (? or :name), so SQLite treats them as data, never as part of the SQL. The only part built from input is the ORDER BY column, which can't be a parameter, so it is chosen from the fixed SORT_COLUMNS dictionary. A test searches for ' OR '1'='1 and checks nothing matches.

keyConcepts.label: ORDER BY from a fixed list

viva.question: What is CSRF and how does your app prevent it?
viva.answer: Cross-site request forgery is when another website makes your browser submit a form to this app, for example to delete a student, using your session. Each session gets a random token, every form includes it in a hidden field, and check_csrf() refuses any POST whose token doesn't match, with 400. The session cookie also uses SameSite=Lax.

viva.question: How do you validate input?
viva.answer: validate_student() and validate_course() in validation.py are pure functions: they clean the input, for example trimming spaces and upper-casing roll numbers, and return the cleaned values and a dictionary of errors by field. The view shows the form again with the typed values, an error summary and a message under each field. The database repeats key rules with UNIQUE and CHECK constraints.

viva.question: What happens if two students get the same roll number?
viva.answer: The roll_number column is UNIQUE COLLATE NOCASE, so SQLite refuses the second insert, even if only the letter case differs. create_student() catches the IntegrityError, recognises the column from the message and raises DuplicateError, which the view shows as an error under the roll number field.

viva.question: Why is deleting done with a POST form instead of a link?
viva.answer: GET requests must not change data: browsers prefetch links and crawlers follow them, and a link can't carry the CSRF token. The Delete link opens a confirmation page; only the form on it, sent with POST and the token, deletes.

viva.question: What is the Post/Redirect/Get pattern and why do you use it?
viva.answer: After a successful POST the view redirects instead of rendering a page. If the user reloads, the browser repeats the GET, not the POST, so nothing is added twice. flash() carries the confirmation message to the next page.

viva.question: How does the student search work?
viva.answer: list_students() adds a WHERE condition that matches the full name, the roll number or the email with LIKE. The search text is turned into a pattern by like_pattern(), which escapes % and _ so they're matched literally. Class and status filters add more conditions, and the total is counted before one page is fetched with LIMIT and OFFSET.

viva.question: How is pagination done?
viva.answer: With LIMIT and OFFSET: LIMIT is the page size from app_config.json and OFFSET is (page - 1) × page size. A separate COUNT(*) gives the total, from which the number of pages is calculated. Asking for a page past the end redirects to the last page.

viva.question: How is the attendance percentage calculated?
viva.answer: The number of marks that are present or late, divided by the number of marks recorded, times 100, rounded to one decimal place. In SQL it's SUM(CASE WHEN status IN ('present', 'late') THEN 1 ELSE 0 END). With no marks it shows “No marks yet” instead of 0%.

viva.question: What is an upsert and where do you use it?
viva.answer: An insert that updates the existing row when the key already exists. save_attendance() uses INSERT … ON CONFLICT (student_id, course_id, date) DO UPDATE SET status = excluded.status, so marking the same day again changes the marks instead of failing.

viva.question: What is create_app() and why use an application factory?
viva.answer: create_app() builds the Flask app: settings, database path, secret key, commands, security checks, blueprints and error pages. A factory lets each test build a fresh app with its own temporary database and a fixed date, instead of sharing one global app with real data.

viva.question: What are blueprints?
viva.answer: A blueprint groups related routes. The app has four: dashboard, students, courses and attendance, each in its own file under studentms/views/ with a URL prefix such as /students. create_app() registers them, which keeps each area's code together.

viva.question: What is the secret key for and how is it kept safe?
viva.answer: Flask signs the session cookie with it; the session holds the CSRF token and flash messages, so anyone with the key could forge them. secret_key() uses SECRET_KEY from the environment if set, otherwise creates a random key once in instance/secret_key, readable only by your own account from the moment it is created. The instance folder is in .gitignore, so the key is never committed.

viva.question: The app only listens on 127.0.0.1. Can a website still reach it, and how does the app stop that?
viva.answer: Yes, with DNS rebinding: a website points a name it controls at 127.0.0.1, so its scripts can open this app's pages and, with a token from the page they read, send its forms. There is no login to stop them. create_app() sets Flask's TRUSTED_HOSTS from trusted_hosts(), so a request whose Host header isn't 127.0.0.1 or localhost is refused with 400 before any page runs. When HOST makes the app listen on the network, any name is accepted, because people may use any of the computer's addresses.

viva.question: What stops a student's name from running as a script in the page?
viva.answer: Jinja escapes everything inserted with {{ }}, so <script> becomes <script> and is shown as text; a test checks this. The Content-Security-Policy also has script-src 'none', so the browser wouldn't run a script even if one got in.

viva.question: How did you test the project?
viva.answer: With pytest. Each test builds the app with a temporary database and a fixed date. There are tests for every validation rule, the configuration, the queries, constraints and cascades, every page through Flask's test client including CSRF tokens, the database commands, and security: escaping, SQL injection attempts and headers.

viva.question: What is the /health route for?
viva.answer: It answers {"status": "ok"} after reading the students table, so a script can tell that the app has started and the database works. CampusKit's verification starts the generated app and waits for it.

viva.question: What are the limitations of your project?
viva.answer: There's no login, so anyone who can open the app can change records. Flask's development server and SQLite suit one user on one computer, not a public website. Attendance is one mark per course per day, times are shown in UTC, and there's no import or export.

viva.question: How would you add a login?
viva.answer: Add a users table with a username and a password hash from werkzeug.security.generate_password_hash, never the plain password. A login form checks the hash with check_password_hash and stores the user id in the session. A before_request check redirects anyone not logged in to the login page.

viva.question: What would you change to let many people use it at once?
viva.answer: Run it with a production WSGI server such as Gunicorn or Waitress behind HTTPS, add a login with roles, and move to a database server like PostgreSQL, which handles many simultaneous writers better than one SQLite file. The repository functions would need little change because all SQL is in one place.

entries.title: “Address already in use” or the page shows something else on port 5000
entries.symptom: python run.py stops with OSError: [Errno 48] Address already in use (or [WinError 10048]), or http://127.0.0.1:5000/ opens a different program.
causes: Another program uses port 5000. On macOS, AirPlay Receiver listens on it.
The app is already running in another terminal.

diagnose.text: Check whether another terminal is already running the app, and stop it with Ctrl+C.

fix.text: Start the app on another port, then open that port in the browser, for example http://127.0.0.1:5050/.

entries.confirm: The dashboard opens at the new address.

entries.title: “ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'flask'”
entries.symptom: python run.py or python -m pytest stops straight away with ModuleNotFoundError for flask or studentms.
causes: The virtual environment isn't active in this terminal.
pip install -r requirements.txt hasn't been run in this environment.
The command was run from another folder, so studentms can't be found.

diagnose.text: The prompt starts with (.venv) when the environment is active. Check which Python runs.

fix.text: Open a terminal in the project folder, activate the environment and install the requirements.

entries.title: “The form expired or didn’t come from this app”
entries.symptom: Submitting a form shows a page with status 400 saying the form expired or didn't come from this app.
causes: The page was opened before the app restarted with a new secret key, so its CSRF token no longer matches.
Cookies are blocked for 127.0.0.1, so the session (and its token) isn't kept.
The form was changed and no longer includes the hidden csrf_token field.

diagnose.text: Reload the form page and submit it again. If it still fails, check that the browser allows cookies for 127.0.0.1.

fix.text: Go back, reload the page and submit again. If you edited a template, make sure every POST form includes <input type="hidden" name="csrf_token" value="{{ csrf_token() }}">.

entries.confirm: The form saves and shows a confirmation message.

entries.title: “sqlite3.OperationalError: database is locked”
entries.symptom: Saving fails with a 500 error page, and the terminal shows sqlite3.OperationalError: database is locked.
causes: Another program has instance/students.db open with unsaved changes, such as DB Browser for SQLite.
A second copy of the app is writing at the same moment.

diagnose.text: Close other programs that have the database open, or press Write Changes or Revert Changes in DB Browser for SQLite.

fix.text: Close the other program, then try again. Keep one copy of the app running at a time.

entries.confirm: Saving works and shows a confirmation message.

entries.title: I want the sample data back, or an empty database
entries.symptom: The database has test records you don't want, or you want to start from the sample class again.
causes: Records added while trying out the app stay in instance/students.db.

diagnose.text: Decide whether to keep a copy: reset-db always saves a backup in instance/backups first.

fix.text: Reset with the sample data, or with --empty for an empty database. Stop the app first.

entries.confirm: After starting the app again, the dashboard shows 12 students (or the empty-database message).

entries.title: “ConfigError: … must be …” when starting
entries.symptom: python run.py stops with studentms.config.ConfigError, for example "students_per_page" must be a whole number from 5 to 50.
causes: A value in app_config.json is the wrong type or out of range.
app_config.json isn't valid JSON, for example because of a missing comma or quote.

diagnose.text: The message names the setting, or the line for a JSON syntax error.

fix.text: Correct the value in app_config.json: text in quotes, whole numbers without quotes, true or false in lower case.

entries.confirm: python run.py starts and the dashboard opens.

entries.title: PowerShell won't run Activate.ps1
entries.symptom: On Windows, .venv\Scripts\Activate.ps1 fails with “running scripts is disabled on this system”.
causes: PowerShell's execution policy blocks scripts by default.

fix.text: Allow scripts you run for your own account (Set-ExecutionPolicy -Scope CurrentUser RemoteSigned, once), or use Command Prompt and run .venv\Scripts\activate.bat instead.
